text: Cut every word that carries no fact or no step; padding such as 'the fact that' goes first.
check: Each cut leaves the facts intact (facts-preserved), and no 'the fact that', 'in order to' or 'at this point in time' is left.

text: Use the active voice, so the reader sees who does what: 'I wrote 60 help articles', not '60 help articles were written'.
check: No passive sentence hides an actor that the original or the CV names.

text: Say the action with its verb, not with a noun hiding the verb: 'we analysed the tickets', not 'we conducted an analysis of the tickets'.
check: slop-lint OFI-01 does not fire where the genre turns it on; no 'conduct an', 'carry out the' or 'make a decision' before a noun in -tion, -ment or -ance.

text: Prefer the specific claim to the general one: a number, a name or a date from the CV says more than an adjective.
check: Every claim about results carries a figure, a name or a date that is in the original or the CV (no-new-facts).

text: Alternate short and long sentences; a run of sentences of the same length reads flat.
check: slop-lint EST-11 does not fire on a text of eight or more sentences.

text: Put the most important thing first, the request or the news, and let the detail follow.
check: The first sentence names what the writer asks for or reports; no 'I hope this email finds you well' before it.

text: Choose the short common word over the formal one: 'use' over 'utilise', 'start' over 'commence', 'enough' over 'sufficient'.
check: No formal word replaced a plain one of the original; the judge's register-fit rubric holds.

text: Write to the reader as 'you', one person to another, and drop throat-clearing such as 'please note'.
check: No 'please note', 'kindly be advised' or 'it should be noted that' is left.

text: Use the exact word, not a near one, and keep the style simple and straight.
check: No word of the original was swapped for a vaguer or fancier near-synonym.

text: Do not imitate the period language of the literary sources: no archaic words or eighteenth-century spelling.
check: S6 finds none of the terms; the judge's literary-contamination rubric flags any other archaism.

text: Take Twain's economy, never his dialect: no spelled-out accents, dropped letters or folksy grammar.
check: S6 finds none of the terms; the judge's literary-contamination rubric holds.

text: Take Bierce's concision, never his tone: no sneer, no scolding and no joke at the reader's expense.
check: The judge's register-fit rubric finds no sardonic aside the original did not have.

text: Do not build long periods of chained clauses; when a sentence carries two ideas, split it.
check: No sentence of the rewrite is longer than the longest sentence of the original.

text: Do not borrow the mood of a story: no melancholy, no lyrical scene-setting and no drama in a message about work.
check: The judge's literary-contamination rubric finds no tragic or lyrical turn the original did not have.

text: Open on the reader, not on yourself: the role, the need or the plan of theirs that made you write, taken from the original or the posting, before any achievement of yours.
check: The first paragraph names the reader's organisation, role, need or the earlier contact, using only what the original or the posting says, and no achievement or metric of the writer appears before it.

text: Say in one plain sentence what you want to bring them or help them with, such as 'I'd like to help with that', before you give the evidence; it states an intention and adds no fact.
check: Before the first achievement there is one sentence of intention that points at the reader's need; it holds no number, client, tool or result that the original or the CV lacks (facts-preserved).

text: Put each achievement next to the need of theirs it answers, in the same sentence or the one before; an achievement told for its own sake reads like the CV.
check: Every sentence with an achievement or a metric is tied, by a clause or by the sentence before it, to a need, requirement or plan of the reader named in the text; no bare list of achievements without a lead-in.

text: The letter is not the CV in fewer words: it gives what the CV cannot, why you are writing to them, what you want to do there and how one example relates to their need, and leaves the rest of the history to the CV.
check: Judge question: does the text give the reader something the CV alone does not (the reason for writing, the intention, the link between an example and their need), or is it the CV in fewer words? A rewrite that only lists CV items fails.

text: Lead into your experience with a short bridge that says why you are telling it, and link one paragraph to the next with a word that carries the logic (so, also, that is why); a transition that links nothing is filler.
check: A bridge sentence that refers to the reader's need or to the intention comes before the first achievement; each transition names a relation between the parts it joins, and slop-lint reports no stock filler opener.

text: In a first contact, close with a polite, open offer: you are happy to talk or to send more, at a time that suits them. Do not set the day for them or announce that you will call.
check: In a first contact the last paragraph names no fixed weekday, date or hour chosen by the writer and no 'I'll call you'; it offers availability or more information and thanks the reader. A day the original already agreed with the reader stays.

text: A follow-up first recalls the earlier contact and what it was about, then adds the one thing left to say and asks lightly about the next step or the timeline they gave.
check: The first sentence refers to the previous message or conversation; the close asks about the next step or the timeline without a deadline set by the writer.

text: Be warm and courteous without selling: thank the reader, keep a confident and friendly tone, and let the facts speak instead of praise of yourself.
check: The text thanks the reader or acknowledges their time once; no self-praise without a fact behind it ('passionate', 'highly skilled', 'results-driven'); the judge's same-voice rubric holds.

text: A cover letter has room for three to five short paragraphs, about one page; spend it on the why, the intention and the links, not on more CV items, and stop before it is longer than the reader will read.
check: The cover letter stays within one page (about 400 words at most) and the words it gains over the original go to the opening, the intention and the bridges, never to facts the original lacks.
